extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing USPTO SME procedure)
extracted.subtask_description: A stepwise worksheet to analyze a single patent claim for subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 using the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (identify invention, determine statutory category, detect judicial exceptions, and evaluate whether claim as a whole amounts to significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim. (MPEP 2103(I))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a separate worksheet for each claim. It is suggested the worksheet be used with the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance Quick Reference Sheet, which includes an overview, flowchart, and form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter) (Step 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B: A. If yes, continue with SME analysis. B. If no, make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record. If no amendment is possible, conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)?
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is 'directed' to an exception when the law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim. For this analysis, it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have identified laws of nature and natural phenomena to include naturally occurring principles/substances and products lacking markedly different characteristics. Abstract ideas include, by example, fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Refer to the case law chart and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. Choose A, B, or C: A. No — conclude SME analysis. B. Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — claim is self-evidently not focused on an exception and does not tie-up the exception; conclude SME analysis. C. Yes — identify limiting elements that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception; then continue SME analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: For product-of-nature exceptions: explain marked-difference analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'products of nature' exceptions, explain why the claimed nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics compared to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a product-of-nature exception, the examiner should explain why the claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics versus the natural counterpart; use case law and the guidance materials to support the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: If Step 2A indicates the claim is directed to an exception, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea and explain the reason(s) they are considered a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the specific limitation(s) and provide a rationale explaining how those limitation(s) map to the judicial exception (fill-in fields provided in the worksheet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Presence of additional elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the exception identified in Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1. No — there are no other elements in the claim in addition to the exception; conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Also consider whether elements in the disclosure could be added to render the claim eligible and identify them for possible suggestion to applicant. 2. Yes — list the claim elements in addition to the exception and continue the SME analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the significance of additional elements (search for an 'inventive concept')
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify additional elements and evaluate their significance to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception (i.e., contains an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what applicant invented (Section I) and how that relates to the additional elements. Evaluate the identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they provide significantly more than the judicial exception. Use the following illustrative reasons (next entries) to support significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: improves another technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: One basis for significance is that the additional elements 'improves another technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's additional elements produce a technological improvement outside the abstract idea (or other exception), that supports a finding of 'significantly more.' Document how the improvement is concrete and specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: improves the functioning of a computer itself
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that 'improves the functioning of a computer itself' can indicate significance, provided it is not merely a generic computer performing generic computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The improvement must be to the computer's functioning (concrete and specific), not just the application of the abstract idea on a generic computer. Avoid concluding significance based on generic implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: applies the exception with/by a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine can support that the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not satisfied by a generic computer performing generic functions. Do not accept 'apply it' or equivalent language as sufficient. The machine must play a specific, meaningful role beyond generic implementation or mere instructions to implement the abstract idea on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing supports significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the concrete transformation (physical or otherwise recognized by precedent) and explain how it differs from mere data manipulation or abstract concept execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: adds a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, and conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field can show the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat appended well-understood, routine, and conventional activities specified at a high level of generality as sufficient. Also note that merely using a generic computer to perform these activities is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: adds unconventional steps confining claim to a particular useful application
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application may indicate significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The steps must be more than insignificant extrasolution activity (for example, mere data gathering). Show how the unconventional steps meaningfully limit the claim to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional-element significance: adds meaningful limitations beyond merely linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Add meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how limitations are meaningful (concrete, specific) rather than a generic statement that the abstract concept is performed in a particular technological context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude SME analysis and appropriate next actions (if elements amount to significantly more or not)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any elements, individually or in combination, amount to the claim reciting significantly more than the exception, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements. If not, make a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If concluding a §101 rejection, use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (or 7.05.01 where indicated). The worksheet provides a sample rejection template: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more.' Include the identified exception and explain why additional elements are not sufficient. Consider clarifying remarks in the Office action about claim interpretation if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and identify disclosure elements that could be added to render claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where additional elements currently in the disclosure (but not the claim) could supply an inventive concept or meaningful limitations, specify those elements in the record and consider proposing amendments to the applicant that might overcome a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident and the claimed invention is not focused on an exception and does not tie up the exception, a streamlined analysis may be appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when a streamlined analysis is appropriate. If using the streamlined analysis, document the basis for concluding the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up the exception such that others cannot practice it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/formal guidance: worksheet and form paragraph use
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative instructions on use of the worksheet and the appropriate form paragraphs when issuing rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of this worksheet is optional. When issuing §101 rejections reference Form Paragraphs 7.05, 7.05.01, and 7.05.015 available in Custom OACs as appropriate. Make assumptions clear in the record when continuing analysis under hypothetical amendments.
